lesson.title: The Glue Holding Ionic Crystals Together
lesson.summary: Lattice energy measures how strongly a crystal of oppositely charged ions holds itself together, and it explains why some ionic compounds are far more stable and higher melting than others.
lesson.body:
Every grain of table salt is a three-dimensional lattice of sodium and chloride ions locked into fixed positions by electrostatic attraction, and lattice energy is the number that tells you exactly how tightly that lattice is held together. Building on the idea of a crystal lattice as the repeating, ordered arrangement of ions in an ionic solid, lattice energy is defined as the energy released when one mole of gaseous cations and one mole of gaseous anions come together to form one mole of the solid crystal. Because bringing oppositely charged particles together always lowers the system's potential energy, this process is exothermic, so lattice energy is reported as a large negative number. Run the process backward, ripping the solid apart into isolated gaseous ions, and you need to supply exactly that much energy back in, an endothermic step of equal magnitude and opposite sign. This mirrors bond formation energy in covalent molecules: forming a stable, lower energy arrangement of particles releases energy, and breaking that arrangement apart costs the same amount back.

What determines how large lattice energy is? Coulomb's law gives the answer directly. The strength of attraction between two ions is proportional to the product of their charges divided by the distance between their centers, so lattice energy scales with the charge of the cation times the charge of the anion, divided by the sum of the two ionic radii. Bigger charges pull harder. Smaller ions let opposite charges get closer together, which also pulls harder. Both effects push in the same direction: highly charged, small ions build the strongest lattices.

Compare sodium chloride and magnesium oxide to see this in action. In NaCl, Na+ and Cl- each carry a single charge, and the lattice energy is about negative 787 kilojoules per mole. In MgO, Mg2+ and O2- each carry a double charge, and the two ions are actually similar in size to Na+ and Cl-. Because charge appears as a product in Coulomb's law, doubling both charges roughly quadruples the attraction, since 2 times 2 equals 4, and the slightly shorter Mg to O distance tightens the attraction even further. The measured lattice energy of MgO comes out to roughly negative 3800 kilojoules per mole, nearly five times more negative than NaCl, exactly the trend Coulomb's law predicts.

Lattice energy is not just an abstract number, it shows up directly in everyday physical properties. A more negative lattice energy means the ions are harder to pull apart, so the solid tends to have a higher melting point and greater hardness. Sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees Celsius, respectable for a solid, but magnesium oxide does not melt until 2852 degrees Celsius, because its lattice is so much more strongly bound. This is also why magnesium oxide is used as a refractory lining in high temperature furnaces while table salt is not.

One practical wrinkle is that lattice energy cannot be measured by a single direct experiment, since nobody can watch a solid vaporize cleanly into separated gaseous ions. Instead, chemists calculate it indirectly using a Born-Haber cycle, which stitches together other measurable energies, including the ionization energies needed to form the gaseous cations and the electron affinities involved in forming the gaseous anions, both of which are covered in the sections on cation and anion formation that follow this one.
